Personal-First Humanism

Borrow Fire, Then Become Fire · MAIN SEQUENCE 02 / 18

Starting point: borrowed fire and the becoming of agents

Make the ethical premise explicit: tools and cooperation support concrete lives; output volume does not substitute for development.

Home · 简体中文

A person encounters an arrangement made for people in general. Something important in their life has no place in it. Making that difference intelligible can begin the work of changing the arrangement.

A philosophy for personal practice begins somewhere concrete: someone perceives, understands, desires, makes, and lives through the consequences. Categories such as user, worker, reader, and citizen make some relations available. The person also brings circumstances and possibilities that those categories may leave unexpressed. Personal-first humanism names an ethical orientation for developing arrangements from that concrete encounter.

Its practical premise is explicit: people's developing understanding, voluntary agency, and ability to sustain worthwhile lives should give tools and cooperative arrangements their direction. A personal philosophy can help articulate what that premise means here, while a model helps give it working form. Actual consequences can then revise the arrangement and its account of the person.

Real persons, revisable descriptions

Taking the person seriously does not require an exhaustive metaphysical theory of personhood. It requires acknowledging the actual life to which a description answers: embodied conditions, experiences, relations, commitments, and effects that continue beyond the description. A model of someone can be inadequate even when it is internally coherent. Their correction can disclose that inadequacy; subsequent experience can disclose another.

The framework takes physical reality as its common ground. Thinking, psychological experience, and engineering are activities within that reality; tools require materials and energy, and bodies live through their consequences. Modest naturalism names the accompanying stance of inquiry: begin with concrete embodied beings and worldly processes, investigating their relations through experience and evidence. A computational account abstracts relations relevant to the question. This leaves particular realization mechanisms and the possibility of a complete reduction of experience to their own inquiries.

“The person is real” therefore has a practical force here. A category, metric, or story does not exhaust the one who lives through its application. Its consequences belong in the assessment. The same force applies to other people; the encounter has more than one center of concern.

Construction, nominalism, and fiction

The possibility of constructing a concept invites questions about what it represents and how it is used. A nominalist question concerns the status of universals and general categories. Hobbes's Leviathan, chapter IV, supplies one historical formulation by treating universal names as applying to individual things [1]. Such a formulation does not make those particulars disappear.

Fictionalism raises another question: could a discourse be useful without accepting its apparent claims as literally true? A selected fictional role can organize conduct; a thought experiment can develop consequences under imagined conditions. Their occurrence and effects are actual even when the represented situation is invented. The metaphor essay develops how expressive constructions become interpretations and realizations.

These distinctions leave room to consider the stronger conditional: if many of the concepts through which we organize life are constructed or treated as fictions, which constructions should we choose? That question makes their adequacy important. It does not establish that everything is fiction. Nor does it derive an ethical answer from an ontological label. A construction could serve administration, efficiency, conformity, discovery, or an individual's development. Choosing among these directions requires reasons about what should matter.

The personal-first premise supplies such a reason: concepts and arrangements should support actual persons' understanding and agency, and remain open to their corrections. Constructibility gives revision room; the ethical premise gives revision a direction. The two contributions should remain distinguishable.

Four connected axes

This proposal can be positioned through four questions. Their working names articulate an orientation, not a completed universal system:

Axis Working orientation What it asks of the practice
Ontology Modest naturalism; concrete persons, natural conditions, processes, and events. Which objects and relations must the account acknowledge, and what resists its description?
Epistemology Fallible inquiry beginning with embodied experience and corrected through feedback. Which observations support or challenge an interpretation, and what distinguishes alternatives?
Value Personal-first humanism. Whose understanding, agency, and worthwhile activity does the arrangement support?
Methodology Question-relative pluralism. Which combination of analogy, formalization, simulation, participation, and experiment answers this question?

These four axes use the same distinctions as Core view YY-09. Value articulates what is worth pursuing; an ontological description, factual judgment, or effective method cannot simply replace it. Practice brings these distinctions together in action and encounters their consequences; instructions, tools, files, and interfaces are concrete realizations. Practice is neither another name for value nor a fifth item that must be placed alongside the four axes.

Computational ontology can participate across these axes in different functions. It articulates objects and changes; it organizes evidence and candidate inferences; it makes selected purposes explicit; and it supplies representations that tools can use. Its reach does not collapse the questions into one. A well-formed representation can still explain the phenomenon poorly, and a predictive model can still serve a purpose we have reason to reject.

“Begin with psychological adequacy before formal refinement” expresses a useful research direction when the question concerns a psychological phenomenon: recognize what needs explanation, then let formal tools clarify and test the candidate structure. The activities can interleave. Adequacy means addressing the phenomenon, including differences that an interpretation fails to explain. It does not mean making someone comfortable through flattering agreement. Mathematical validity and empirical adequacy retain their distinct checks.

Preferences can choose a question, direct attention, or guide the adoption of a working view. Evidence constrains what can be accepted as true about its object. Intuition and abduction can propose a candidate before all its conditions are explicit; comparison and feedback can develop or defeat it. This is why the epistemological name above emphasizes a starting point and corrigibility.

Adapt arrangements around people

A personal-first design asks how a difficulty is produced before asking the person to absorb it. Some difficulties can be changed through a cooperative arrangement: when work happens, how decisions are shared, or what others need to receive. Others call for different software or an interface. A person can also choose to learn, practice, or change a habit for an end they recognize.

Considering social arrangements and software before demanding personal adaptation is a productive direction. It opens alternatives that a fixed environment might conceal. Actual dependencies can require another order; the question is which change serves the purpose under the circumstances.

For instance, an explanatory assistant might send every investigative detail to the reader. Instead of treating the reader's overload as a defect to train away, the collaborators can redesign the explanation around the judgment the reader needs to make. The model can carry retrieval and implementation while making reasons, alternatives, and material uncertainty intelligible. The person participates through recognition, questioning, and decisions that matter. If the purpose is learning the investigative method, the allocation can change.

The improvement should be assessed through actual work: can the person understand the choice, influence its direction, and use what is produced? Output volume and the model's reassurance are different observations.

Society is an encounter among persons

Society includes institutions and norms that shape what people can do. It also includes other persons with their own purposes, needs, and contributions. A philosophy more adequate to one individual can improve shared arrangements by revealing an overlooked possibility. It can also impose costs on others. Those effects belong to its assessment.

Mill's On Liberty, chapter III, argues for individuality and different experiments of living while retaining the condition of not injuring others [2]. This offers a source for the connection between singular development and plural coexistence. The present proposal develops it through revisable tools and model-supported practices.

A common framework can enable people to cooperate without demanding identical lives. Standards, stable interfaces, and shared procedures can protect useful continuity; they should also be open to criticism where their effects defeat their purposes. A person's disagreement is an occasion to investigate the relation, not automatic evidence that every social constraint is harmful.

Models contribute to that inquiry as interpreting and generating counterparts. Their participation can enlarge human agency while retaining independent judgment. Personal-first humanism chooses a purpose for the arrangement; it does not require the person to author every idea or perform every step. The Sun–Moon–Earth composition keeps these contributions and the independent world together.

A changing person in a changing world

A person's understanding develops while tools and social conditions can also change. A representation adequate to an earlier encounter may need revision because the question, capabilities, or conditions have changed. Preserving continuity means retaining what still serves the practice while making such differences recognizable.

Carnap's account of framework adoption attends to purpose, fruitfulness, and the effort involved in using a linguistic form [3]. It provides a comparison for this choice among representations. The embodied experimental essay connects their selection with participation and later evidence. A system can support reasoning; reflection can also examine its boundary and aim. Dynamic representation and model selection are resources in this work, rather than proof that any one account contains the whole life.

Return to the person whose life had no place in a general arrangement. Success need not mean that the person has learned to fit the old category. An explanation may become intelligible, a tool usable, or a different way of cooperating sustainable. The person may also choose a demanding change in themselves. Humanism gives these transformations their measure: what understanding, voluntary agency, and worthwhile activity do they make possible, and what do they ask of other lives?

Sources and scope

Modest naturalism, the four-axis positioning, and their model-supported realization are this essay's synthesis. The sources contribute the distinctions identified above; the ethical orientation is argued here and remains open to criticism and inquiry through its consequences.

  1. Thomas Hobbes (1651), Leviathan, chapter IV, “Of Speech.” Original text. One historical account of universal names and particular things, not a proof of the present ethical orientation.
  2. John Stuart Mill (1859), On Liberty, chapter III. Original text. Individuality and experiments of living within plural coexistence.
  3. Rudolf Carnap (1950), Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology. Public reprint. Purpose-sensitive adoption of linguistic frameworks; the personal-first premise is supplied separately here.
